text:
Zero Breach Toolkit

 Version 3 is out: besides looking for known spyware, it now shows the ways in left open on your devices,
 checks the links, emails, files and QR codes people send you, and walks you through your accounts and home
 network. A double-click app for Windows, Mac and Linux, in 27 languages.
 Download it from the latest release.

 Your antivirus may delete the program without asking. Microsoft Defender and other antivirus
 products sometimes wrongly remove new programs that are not code-signed yet. If the download vanishes,
 will not open, or you see "Threat found", it is a false alarm when the file came from the official
 release page. See If your antivirus removes it for safe ways round it. Checking a phone?
 The browser check needs no download at all.

A free, open-source check for traces of known mercenary spyware (Pegasus, Predator,
Graphite, Candiru and others) on computers, Android phones and iPhone backups.

- Read-only. It does not modify source evidence or system settings. It writes only
 temporary database snapshots and the reports you ask for.
- No network requests during a scan. It never looks up spyware addresses and has no
 upload feature. Python network calls are blocked and redirected paths are refused. This
 is not an operating-system network sandbox; see PRIVACY.md.
- States its limits. Every report says what was found, how strong the evidence is, and
 what could not be checked. A clean result is never presented as proof that you are safe.

Made by archivegenocide. Built on Zero Breach.

 If you think you are being targeted right now, get expert help first. You do not
 need to run this tool before asking. Journalists, activists, human-rights defenders and
 civil society can contact the
 Access Now Digital Security Helpline (free, 24/7,
 many languages) or Amnesty International's Security Lab.

---

 Phone backup? Check it in your browser

To check an iPhone backup or an Android collection there is nothing to install: open
archivegenocide.com/scan/phone on the computer that holds
the backup, choose the backup folder, and you get the same result as the program, in your language.
Nothing is uploaded. The check runs inside a part of the page whose security settings forbid every
network connection, and before it opens your backup it proves this by trying to reach the site and
showing you that your browser blocked it. The page's code is in web/phone/ .

A web page cannot look at the computer itself (its programs, start-up items and connections). To
check a computer, use the program below.

 Easiest: download the program (no Python, no commands)

 You do not need to know anything technical to use this. Download one file from the
latest release, open it,
and follow the window. You do not need the source code on this page, and you do not need to
type any commands.

Once it is open: choose a check, press Start check , and read the result. It tells you in
plain words whether anything was found and what to do next. You can save the report if you
want to keep it or show it to someone helping you.

 Which check? Use Standard unless you have a reason not to: it covers browsers, apps,
startup items, program files and out-of-date programs (usually 15 to 20 minutes). Quick looks
at browsers only (5 to 10 minutes). Full adds web caches and more file types (30 minutes or
more). You can press Stop at any time and keep what has been checked so far. To check a
phone, choose A phone in the window; the guides there explain what you need first.

 A green result is good news, not a guarantee. It means this check found none of the published
traces it looks for, in the places it could read. It cannot find spyware nobody has published
traces of, and it does not prove a device is safe. If you think you are being targeted, ask a
digital-security helpline even if the result is green.

 Your antivirus may flag or delete these programs. It is a false alarm if the file came from the official release page; see If your antivirus removes it. If the file came from anywhere else, do not run it and trust the warning. 

 Windows

1. Download zero-breach-toolkit-windows-x64.exe .
2. Double-click it in your Downloads folder.
3. Windows may say it "protected your PC". Click More info , then Run anyway .
4. If the file disappears, or Windows Security says it found a threat, see
 If your antivirus removes it.

 Mac

1. Download zero-breach-toolkit-macos-apple-silicon.dmg for a newer Mac (M1, M2, M3, M4),
 or zero-breach-toolkit-macos-intel.dmg for an older Intel Mac. The Apple menu →
 About This Mac says which one you have.
2. Open it, drag Zero Breach Toolkit into Applications, then open it from Applications.
3. macOS will refuse the first time. Open System Settings → Privacy & Security , scroll
 down, click Open Anyway , then open the app again.

Open the app on the Mac itself, not through a remote or SSH session: it needs a desktop.

 Linux

1. Download zero-breach-toolkit-linux-x64.tar.gz .
2. Extract it (double-click it, or tar -xzf zero-breach-toolkit-linux-x64.tar.gz ).
3. Run ./zero-breach-toolkit , or right-click it and choose Run in Terminal .

The warnings appear because the programs are not signed by Microsoft or Apple yet. Each
program is built by GitHub from the published source, and you can check that before running it:
 gh attestation verify --repo interplains/Zero-Breach-Toolkit (see
docs/VERIFYING.md). Prefer to see exactly what runs? Use the Python
version in the guide below; it is the same check.

To let the check read Safari on a Mac, give Zero Breach Toolkit (or Terminal, for the Python
version) Full Disk Access in System Settings → Privacy & Security.

New programs that are not code-signed yet are often flagged by mistake, and some antivirus products
delete them straight away without asking. If you downloaded the program from

install.title: Install and run
install.html:
You need Python 3.8 or newer (python.org; on Windows, tick "Add python.exe to PATH" when installing). No administrator rights and no extra packages. On macOS and Linux type python3 instead of python.

  1. Get the toolkit. On GitHub choose Code → Download ZIP and extract it, or:
    git clone https://github.com/interplains/Zero-Breach-Toolkit.git
  2. Open a terminal in the toolkit folder. Windows: open the extracted folder (Zero-Breach-Toolkit, or Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main from a ZIP), click the address bar, type powershell and press Enter. macOS: open Terminal, type cd (with a space), drag the folder into the window and press Enter. Run every command below from this folder.
  3. Recommended: download the latest indicator lists. This is optional and is the only step that uses the internet; the checks themselves never do. Without it only a small built-in set is used. Repeat it every few weeks.
    python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --update
  4. On a Mac, give Terminal Full Disk Access first (System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access → add Terminal, then reopen it). Without it macOS blocks Safari's records and some folders, and the report lists them as not checked.
  5. Close your browsers and chat apps, then run the check. A menu opens; press Enter for the standard check of this computer.
    python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py
    On Windows you can instead double-click scan\run-scan.cmd. It saves the readable and JSON reports in a findings folder next to the toolkit.

Reports contain private details from your computer; keep them out of shared and synced folders. Useful options:

python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --quick                     # faster: skips file fingerprints
python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --phone "FOLDER"            # a phone collection or backup
python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --json report.json          # machine-readable report
python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --share-json summary.json   # minimal summary for sharing

Put folder paths in quotes, especially if they contain spaces. On Linux or macOS, sh scan/run-scan.sh takes the same options.

Verify what you run

The project is anonymous, so do not take its word for anything. Verification rests on what you can reproduce.

Running from source, as above, means every line the tool executes is in the clone: nothing is compiled and nothing is fetched in order to run.

The single-file zero-breach-toolkit.py attached to a release is generated from the same source. Rebuild it from the release's tag and compare:

git checkout v3.0.2
python build/bundle.py
python -c "import hashlib; print(hashlib.sha256(open('dist/zero-breach-toolkit.py','rb').read()).hexdigest())"

For v3.0.2 the file is 7,879,062 bytes, SHA-256 0b6df5f02c6b13256b735bfb55c1ef0a31ff0c762550910be9f66b4f5090dafb. The size and SHA-256 published with each release are authoritative. The build is deterministic, so a matching rebuild means the published file contains that source and nothing else. Releases are also GPG-signed; see docs/VERIFYING.md.

The Windows program is being set up for signing through the SignPath Foundation, whose certificate is issued to the Foundation rather than to a person, so the project stays anonymous; see docs/CODE-SIGNING.md. Until that is in place the program is unsigned. An .exe you build yourself with PyInstaller is unsigned, has no download reputation and is not byte-reproducible, so SmartScreen will warn, some antivirus products will flag it, and the comparison above does not apply. Running from source avoids all of that.

Checking an Android phone

  1. On the phone, turn on Developer options (Settings → About phone → tap Build number seven times), then turn on USB debugging.

  2. Connect the phone by USB and tap Allow when it asks about this computer.

  3. Download and run AndroidQF on the computer. Answer its questions like this:

    AndroidQF asks Answer
    Take a backup of the device? Only SMS
    Download copies of all apps or only non-system ones? Only non-system packages
    Remove copies of apps signed with a trusted certificate? No
    Take the Intrusion Logs? No, unless you turned on Intrusion Logging
    Hash files on the device? No (Yes also checks file fingerprints, but it is slow and can stop the collection on some phones)
    Browser history / Magisk modules? No

    On the phone, confirm the backup with Back up my data.

  4. AndroidQF saves a .zip next to itself. Extract it.

  5. From the toolkit folder, check the extracted folder (keep the quotes):

    python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --phone "PATH TO THE EXTRACTED FOLDER"

    Or run the tool with no options, choose A phone, and drag the folder into the window.

  6. Turn USB debugging off again.

The collection holds private information about the phone. Keep it on your computer.

Use --phone-guide android for preparation steps and --phone FOLDER --preview to list which artifacts are available. For an AES-encrypted backup.ab, add --backup-password; the password is asked for privately at the terminal and never appears as an argument or in a report. Age-encrypted acquisition archives must first be decrypted with the owner's identity using the separate age tool; this scanner does not launch it.

Guided acquisition (experimental). --collect-android LOCAL_OUTPUT_FOLDER downloads official AndroidQF v1.8.3, checks its pinned SHA-256, asks for the device owner's explicit consent and runs the collector's interactive prompts. After a successful plaintext acquisition it extracts the archive locally and checks the collection. Acquisition changes phone state and saves private records; it is separate from read-only scanning.

This is the only point at which the tool runs a program it did not ship:

  • the asset name and expected digest are fixed in the source;
  • the file is fetched over HTTPS from the publisher's release, with redirects limited to an allow-list, and hashed while downloading;
  • if the digest does not match, acquisition is refused and nothing is executed;
  • the collector is written to a temporary directory and run directly, not through a shell, with ADB_, ANDROID_ADB_, LD_ and DYLD_ variables removed and PATH reset to the system directory, then deleted when the command finishes;
  • nothing is downloaded or run unless you invoke the command and confirm consent.

The pinned digest verifies the publisher's release bytes; it is not an independent audit of the collector. The publisher ships the Windows build unsigned, so a browser download shows the usual "not commonly downloaded" warning and SmartScreen prompts on first run. If you prefer, install AndroidQF yourself, follow the five steps above and skip this command.

--age-recipient-file PATH supplies public age1 recipients (private identity files are refused). When encryption is requested, a plaintext result is refused. An encrypted result must have a supported age envelope and no unexpected extra files, but these format checks cannot authenticate it or verify the recipient. It is saved for separate decryption; the command succeeds without producing a scan or an all-clear. After a failure, check the reported folder: original or partial records are kept and may be unencrypted.

Checking local iPhone evidence
  1. Make a local backup with Finder (Mac) or Apple Devices / iTunes (Windows). Tick Encrypt local backup: encrypted backups include more of the records this tool checks.
  2. Find the backup folder (one per device, with Manifest.plist inside): on a Mac ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/, on Windows %USERPROFILE%\Apple\MobileSync\Backup\.
  3. From the toolkit folder (keep the quotes; leave out --backup-password if the backup is not encrypted, and the password is asked for privately):
    python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --phone "PATH TO THE BACKUP FOLDER" --backup-password

--phone-guide ios and --phone-guide android print these steps in the terminal.

usage.title: Practising with a training example
usage.html:
Trainers need a result to show, and real spyware cannot be used for that. --training checks a made-up Android phone against made-up indicators, so people can learn to read a report before they need to. It is also in the start menu as Practise with a training example, and in the window as Practise, where the result carries an amber TRAINING EXAMPLE bar.

python scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --training spyware        # findings and evidence grades
python scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --training worth-a-look   # leads, but no findings
python scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --training clean          # what "nothing found" means
python scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --training cellebrite     # a phone seized and unlocked with Cellebrite

The report is the ordinary report, so what people learn carries over to a real check. It opens with TRAINING EXAMPLE - NOT A REAL CHECK and ends with notes for the trainer; the JSON report has a training field and its first must_relay rule says it is an example.

  • Nothing on the computer, a real phone or a downloaded indicator list is read. Options that point a check at real evidence or real indicators are refused with --training.
  • Every indicator is invented: the domain uses the reserved .invalid ending, which can never exist, and the family is named "Training example (not real spyware)".
  • The cellebrite example is the exception, because its point is to show the real result. Its made-up phone log records one of the fake USB devices Cellebrite's unlocking hardware imitates, which the ordinary phone check recognises by itself. The serial number and the rest of the log are invented.
  • A sharing summary or evidence bundle cannot be made from it, because both are meant to be sent to someone.
  • The example is built in the temporary folder and deleted when the tool exits.
